# Shaping Artifact: Session-Refreshable CLI TLS Trust

## 1. Problem

A long-lived automation session can retain TLS trust from the daemon’s initial invocation. Later operator-selected CA or OS trust settings therefore may not reach direct HTTP reads or other CLI-owned TLS clients unless browser state or the daemon is recreated.

The amendment must make effective TLS trust refreshable independently of browser launch while preserving the daemon process and browser state when trust is unchanged—or changes only in TLS configuration.

## 2. Scope

### In scope

- Direct read URL, including its serialized daemon dispatch path.
- Other CLI-owned outgoing TLS clients.
- Standalone CLI TLS used by install.
- Explicit PEM/DER CA selection and clearing.
- OS trust enablement and explicit disablement.
- Same-path certificate rotation.
- Long-lived session behavior and session isolation.
- CLI/MCP parity.
- Existing local Linux Chromium CA lifecycle and default trust behavior.

### Out of scope

- Browser TLS redesign.
- New certificate parsing heuristics.
- TTL-based refresh.
- Retroactively terminating established TLS operations.
- General platform trust architecture.
- GitHub writes or release work.
- Replacing the existing PEM/DER validation and normalization.
- Implementation in this shaping pass.

---

## 3. Requirements Table

### Settled requirements

| ID | Requirement | Status |
|---|---|---|
| R0 | read URL with a selected CA must complete without launching or configuring a browser, including on macOS and Windows. install must continue using standalone CLI TLS without requiring daemon or browser setup. | Settled |
| R1 | Explicit PEM/DER CA and OS trust selection must reach every CLI-owned outgoing TLS client. Hostname, certificate validity, and unrelated-issuer checks remain enabled. | Settled |
| R2 | A continuing session must observe newly selected CA or OS trust settings. Equivalent CA selection or omission must preserve effective trust, daemon PID, and browser target/URL/page state. TLS-only changes must not discard browser state. | Settled |
| R3 | Explicit CA clear and explicit false for OS trust must differ from omission. Clear must permit return to public-root behavior. An invalid explicit CA must fail visibly and must not allow the command under unintended trust. Invalid ambient SSL_CERT_FILE may warn and fall back. | Settled |
| R4 | Rotation of a certificate bundle at the same path must affect subsequent new TLS operations. OS root changes must be observed on subsequent commands without manually killing the daemon. Established operations may finish; retroactive invalidation is not required. | Settled |
| R5 | Session isolation, CLI/MCP parity, local Linux Chromium CA lifecycle, and default trust behavior must remain intact. | Settled |
| R6 | Work remains local-only in an isolated worktree and preserves prior contributor work. No GitHub write or release. | Settled |

### Derived requirements

| ID | Requirement | Derivation |
|---|---|---|
| R7 | Effective TLS settings must be session-scoped rather than frozen process-initialization state. | Required by R2, R4, and R5. |
| R8 | Incoming options require patch semantics: omission retains the selected source, while explicit clear/false changes it. | Required by R2 and R3. |
| R9 | Retaining a selected source does not mean retaining previously loaded trust material. Before a subsequent command is admitted, an active CA source must be reparsed and an active OS source reloaded. | Required by same-path and OS-root refresh in R4. |
| R10 | Trust identity for explicit CA material must use the certificate parser’s canonical normalized content, not only option text or path. | Required for equivalent-CA continuity and same-path rotation in R2/R4. |
| R11 | Trust publication must be atomic. A command either uses one validated trust snapshot or fails before its new TLS work is admitted. | Required by R3 and by background-client race concerns. |
| R12 | All CLI-owned TLS connection creation must obtain the current session trust snapshot through one shared boundary or provider. Updating only read URL, browser launch, or one HTTP singleton is insufficient. | Required by R0 and R1. |
| R13 | Connections from an older trust generation must not be assigned to operations admitted after a refreshed snapshot is published. Already in-flight operations on established connections may finish. | Precise operational boundary required by R4. |
| R14 | A failed refresh of a previously selected explicit CA source must not silently fall back. The attempted command fails, and the last valid committed session setting remains unchanged. | A retained explicit source remains operator-selected; fallback would violate R3. |
| R15 | TLS trust updates must not invoke browser teardown, target recreation, navigation, or page-state reset. | Required by R2 and separation in R0. |
| R16 | install must reuse the same trust resolution and TLS-client construction rules where applicable, but without daemon session ownership. | Required by R0/R1 while preserving standalone execution. |
| R17 | Session identity must be part of trust-state lookup and publication; one session’s update must not alter another session’s clients. | Required by R5. |
| R18 | Existing Linux Chromium CA handling must remain on its current browser-specific path; the amendment adds CLI TLS propagation rather than replacing browser certificate lifecycle behavior. | Required by R5 and minimal-fix scope. |

### Undecided questions

These are implementation decisions, not additional product requirements.

| ID | Undecided question | Must be learned before implementation |
|---|---|---|
| U1 | Which existing daemon/session object should own effective TLS source selection and the current immutable trust snapshot? | Inspect session and dispatcher ownership boundaries. |
| U2 | What is the actual cost and platform behavior of reloading OS roots at each relevant command boundary? | Measure the existing loaders on supported platforms; do not assume a TTL is needed. |
| U3 | Which background clients can initiate TLS concurrently with command dispatch, and where can they acquire an atomic trust-generation lease? | Inventory connection factories and asynchronous workers. |
| U4 | How should a pre-fix daemon of the same package version be detected or migrated when it lacks the amended protocol/state behavior? | Determine whether an existing capability/version handshake can distinguish behavior. |
| U5 | What are the existing composition and precedence rules when explicit CA and OS trust settings are both active? | Preserve current semantics; do not redefine them in this amendment. |
| U6 | Which commands count as trust-refresh boundaries if they do not themselves appear to perform TLS but can trigger background TLS work? | Trace command admission and background scheduling. |

---

## 4. Required Temporal Model

Trust configuration is a patch over session state, while trust material is refreshed from the retained source.

| Transition | Required result |
|---|---|
| Unset → set | Validate and resolve the selected source, then atomically publish it before admitting new TLS work. |
| Set → omitted | Retain the source selection, but reload/reparse its current material before the command. |
| Set → same | Resolve again. If canonical material and effective settings are equivalent, preserve the effective generation and all continuity observables. |
| Set → same path with rotated contents | Publish a new trust snapshot for subsequent operations without changing daemon or browser state. |
| Set → changed | Validate the replacement first, then atomically publish it. |
| Set → explicit CA clear | Remove the explicit CA selection and restore the existing public-root/default behavior without browser or daemon restart. |
| OS trust set → explicit false | Disable that selection according to existing trust-composition semantics; this is not omission. |
| Set → invalid explicit replacement | Reject visibly; do not publish or admit the command’s new TLS work under fallback trust. |
| Retained explicit source → invalid on refresh | Reject visibly and retain the last committed setting; do not silently treat it as ambient configuration. |
| Invalid ambient SSL_CERT_FILE | Existing warn-and-fallback behavior may continue. |

### Continuity observables

For omission, equivalent CA content, and all TLS-only updates:

- Daemon PID remains unchanged.
- Existing browser target identity remains unchanged.
- Current browser URL remains unchanged.
- Page state remains unchanged.

### TLS operation boundary

A trust snapshot is published before the associated command is admitted.

- TLS operations already in flight on established connections may finish.
- Old-generation connections are retired from reuse after publication.
- Any operation admitted after publication must acquire the current generation and must not receive an old pooled connection.
- No requirement is made to terminate or revalidate an operation already in flight.

---

## 5. Candidate Shapes

## Shape A — Daemon-owned session trust with immutable generations

### Parts

1. Session TLS source state
   - Store the tri-state/patchable CA and OS trust selections on the daemon’s existing session object.
   - Keep this state independent of browser configuration.

2. Command-bound resolution
   - Apply explicit option patches.
   - Retain omitted selections.
   - Reparse retained explicit CA sources and reload retained OS roots before admitting the command.
   - Use the existing certificate parser and canonical normalized content.

3. Immutable trust snapshot
   - Build one validated snapshot containing the effective trust inputs.
   - Compare canonical effective content with the committed snapshot.
   - Publish a new generation only when effective material or explicit state changes.

4. Generation-aware TLS provider
   - Route every daemon-side CLI-owned TLS connection through a shared provider.
   - Each new operation acquires the current session generation.
   - Pools are generation-bound; publication prevents old pools from servicing later operations.

5. Serialized dispatcher integration
   - Resolve and publish before the serialized read URL dispatcher admits the request.
   - Do not condition this work on browser launch or browser availability.

6. Standalone integration
   - install invokes the same resolver/client-construction logic directly with invocation-scoped settings, without creating daemon state.

7. Failure transaction
   - Explicit parse/load failure aborts before publication.
   - The prior committed session setting remains intact.
   - Ambient invalid SSL_CERT_FILE retains its separate warning/fallback behavior.

### Character

A focused amendment to daemon session state and TLS-client construction. Browser lifecycle remains untouched.

---

## Shape B — Frontend-owned durable trust state with full snapshots sent per command

### Parts

1. Persist effective trust source selections in CLI/MCP frontend session storage.
2. Resolve CA files and OS roots on every frontend command.
3. Send a complete trust snapshot rather than a patch to the daemon.
4. Keep the daemon trust-stateless except for generation-bound client pools.
5. Make every frontend use the same persistence, validation, and serialization rules.
6. Have install consume the same frontend resolver.

### Character

Moves temporal ownership out of the daemon. This can satisfy refresh behavior but introduces a second durable session model and requires all frontends to coordinate identically.

---

## Shape C — Stateless per-command trust options

### Parts

1. Apply only options present on the current command.
2. Configure the immediate HTTP client from those options.
3. On omission, use process/default trust.
4. Do not retain session TLS selection.
5. Rebuild only the directly targeted client.

### Character

Smallest apparent code change, but it does not model continuing-session trust semantics.

---

## Shape D — Restart or recreate runtime components on trust changes

### Parts

1. Detect changed trust options.
2. Restart the daemon or recreate browser/runtime clients.
3. Reapply trust at initialization.
4. Attempt to reconnect or restore browser state afterward.

### Character

Reuses initialization behavior but treats TLS refresh as lifecycle replacement.

---

## 6. Binary Fit Check

Y means the shape can satisfy the requirement as described. N means it structurally fails; notes identify the failure.

| Requirement | Shape A | Shape B | Shape C | Shape D |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| R0 browser-independent read and standalone install | Y | Y | Y | N |
| R1 reaches every CLI-owned TLS client | Y | Y | N | N |
| R2 continuing session and continuity | Y | Y | N | N |
| R3 omission/clear/false and explicit-invalid behavior | Y | Y | N | Y |
| R4 same-path and OS-root refresh | Y | Y | N | Y |
| R5 isolation, parity, Linux lifecycle, defaults | Y | Y | N | N |
| R6 local-only shaping scope | Y | Y | Y | Y |
| R7 session-scoped effective state | Y | Y | N | N |
| R8 patch semantics | Y | Y | N | Y |
| R9 retained-source material refresh | Y | Y | N | Y |
| R10 canonical content identity | Y | Y | N | Y |
| R11 atomic validation/publication | Y | Y | N | N |
| R12 shared TLS construction boundary | Y | Y | N | N |
| R13 generation-safe connection reuse | Y | Y | N | N |
| R14 retained explicit-source failure safety | Y | Y | N | Y |
| R15 no browser-state reset | Y | Y | Y | N |
| R16 shared standalone install rules | Y | Y | Y | N |
| R17 session isolation | Y | Y | N | N |
| R18 preserve Chromium CA lifecycle | Y | Y | Y | N |

### Failure notes

- Shape B: No binary requirement failure, but it creates competing session ownership and makes CLI/MCP coordination and daemon reconnection materially more complex.
- Shape C: Omission reverts to defaults instead of retaining effective selection; updates reach only directly modified clients; it cannot safely handle pooled/background clients or session isolation.
- Shape D: Violates the explicit daemon PID and browser-state continuity requirements. Reconnection or attempted page restoration is not equivalent to preserving the existing target and page state.

---

## 7. Survivor

## Shape A — Daemon-owned session trust with immutable generations

Shape A is the minimal correct amendment because the affected read URL path already passes through the long-lived daemon and the required semantics are session-temporal. The daemon is therefore the narrowest existing place that can:

- distinguish omission from explicit clear/false;
- retain source selection across commands;
- refresh material behind a retained source;
- serialize publication before request admission;
- prevent old pooled connections from serving later operations;
- preserve daemon and browser continuity;
- provide the same effective snapshot to background clients.

The standalone install path does not need daemon ownership. It should reuse the resolver and TLS-client builder with invocation-scoped state.

### Non-goals for the survivor

- No browser relaunch.
- No daemon restart.
- No persisted frontend trust database.
- No TTL or watcher system.
- No parser replacement.
- No process-global environment mutation.
- No redefinition of explicit-CA/OS-root composition.
- No retroactive cancellation of established operations.

---

## 8. Rejected Alternatives

### Shape B — Frontend-owned durable state

Rejected despite binary fit because it is not a focused amendment:

- Duplicates session identity and lifecycle outside the daemon.
- Requires CLI and MCP to coordinate durable state perfectly.
- Risks divergence when a frontend reconnects to an existing daemon.
- Complicates multiple clients attached to one daemon session.
- Makes pre-fix daemon compatibility harder to reason about.
- Sends resolved trust material across an additional boundary unnecessarily.

### Shape C — Stateless command options

Rejected because it fails the core temporal requirement:

- Omission cannot retain prior selection.
- Same-path rotation is only noticed when the option is repeated.
- Directly updated clients can diverge from background or pooled clients.
- Explicit clear cannot be distinguished reliably from absence without retained state.

### Shape D — Runtime restart

Rejected because:

- Daemon PID changes.
- Browser target identity and page state can be lost or recreated.
- Browserless direct reads become incorrectly coupled to runtime lifecycle.
- It does not provide the required operation-level boundary for concurrent clients.

### Process-global CA/environment mutation

Also rejected as a variant rather than a complete shape:

- Violates session isolation.
- Cannot safely represent concurrent generations.
- Encourages hidden clients to read mutable global state at inconsistent times.
- Confuses explicit selection with ambient SSL_CERT_FILE.

---

## 9. Forward Risks

| Risk | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Hidden TLS construction sites bypass the shared provider. | Some outgoing clients continue using startup trust. |
| Existing connection pools are not generation-keyed or retired. | A command after refresh may use an old established connection. |
| Snapshot publication occurs after command/background work is scheduled. | Race permits new work under prior trust. |
| Session lookup is incomplete or process-global. | Trust can leak between sessions. |
| Path or option-string equality is used instead of canonical content. | Same-path rotation is missed or equivalent CA input causes unnecessary churn. |
| File changes between validation and snapshot construction. | A command may publish material different from what was validated. |
| OS-root loading has unsupported platform behavior or material cost. | Per-command refresh may regress macOS/Windows behavior or command overhead. |
| Explicit-source load failure is treated like ambient configuration failure. | The command can proceed under unintended public roots. |
| An old-generation pool is closed too aggressively. | Established operations that are allowed to finish may be interrupted. |
| Pre-fix daemon cannot recognize the new trust patch/snapshot protocol. | Same-version client/daemon combinations may silently preserve frozen trust. |
| Shared resolver refactoring crosses into Chromium CA handling. | Local Linux browser certificate lifecycle regresses. |
| CLI and MCP encode omission/clear/false differently. | Frontend parity and temporal semantics diverge. |

---

## 10. Cheapest Falsification Probes

These probes should precede broad implementation.

1. TLS-client inventory
   - Enumerate every CLI-owned TLS client and connection pool.
   - Record whether it is daemon-side, standalone, background, or browser-specific.
   - Falsifies Shape A if important clients cannot acquire session-scoped snapshots through a common boundary.

2. Dispatcher ordering probe
   - Instrument command receipt, trust resolution, snapshot publication, and read URL admission.
   - Verify publication can occur before the serialized dispatcher starts TLS work.

3. State-transition contract test
   - In one daemon session, exercise unset→set, set→omitted, set→same, set→changed, and set→clear.
   - Assert daemon PID and browser target/URL/page markers remain unchanged.

4. Canonical equivalence test
   - Supply equivalent PEM/DER or formatting variants accepted by the existing parser.
   - Verify normalized equivalence causes no browser reset, daemon restart, or unnecessary trust-generation change.

5. Same-path rotation test
   - Replace the bundle contents at an unchanged path with a different valid issuer.
   - Omit the option on the next command.
   - Verify a new connection uses the rotated trust and the old issuer no longer authorizes that new connection.

6. Established-operation boundary test
   - Hold one operation open on an old-generation connection.
   - Publish refreshed trust.
   - Verify the old operation may finish, while a subsequently admitted operation cannot borrow that connection.

7. Invalid explicit refresh test
   - Corrupt a currently selected explicit bundle before the next command.
   - Verify visible command failure, no fallback acceptance, and no publication of a partial snapshot.

8. Ambient-invalid distinction test
   - Use invalid ambient SSL_CERT_FILE without explicit selection.
   - Verify existing warning/fallback behavior remains distinct from explicit-source failure.

9. OS-root reload seam test
   - Substitute or instrument the existing OS-root loader.
   - Verify it is consulted on subsequent commands while selected and that changed material yields a new snapshot.
   - Measure loader cost rather than assuming a cache or TTL.

10. Session-isolation test
    - Run two sessions with mutually exclusive private issuers.
    - Refresh one session and verify the other session’s effective trust and pools remain unchanged.

11. CLI/MCP parity test
    - Apply each patch transition through both entry points.
    - Verify identical omission, clear, false, invalid, and continuity behavior.

12. Standalone install test
    - Run its TLS path with browser and daemon setup unavailable.
    - Verify explicit CA and OS trust behavior still works through invocation-scoped resolution.

13. Pre-fix daemon compatibility probe
    - Connect an amended client to a pre-amendment daemon of the same package version.
    - Determine whether capability negotiation can detect missing refresh semantics.
    - Keep migration behavior undecided until this result is known.

---

## 11. Amendment Boundary

The focused amendment is:

> Add session-scoped, patchable TLS trust source state to the daemon; resolve retained sources at command boundaries; atomically publish immutable, generation-bound trust snapshots to every CLI-owned daemon TLS client; and reuse the same resolver/client builder for standalone install, without coupling any of this to browser launch or lifecycle.

This addresses the known frozen-trust defect without introducing a new platform trust design.
